rationale: B wins because it finds sharper editorial tension and builds proof around the fight, not just the announcement. A's "Liquid Death certifies as a B Corp and says it has given $4.2M" is accurate but sits too close to a company milestone; B's "Liquid Death got B Corp certified. The standard just got a stress test." gives a sustainability reporter an argument to test. The win is slight because B also gets cute with "sells almost no water," which is not in the supplied facts.
gaps_in_A: "event tickets" is invented. The update says the store runs in-store events; it does not say tickets are sold.
"Story type: category-creation" overstates the second store angle. Merch, limited-edition cans, and events may be a brand-retail model, but the update does not support category creation.
"Already in 120,000 stores..." and "first store sells T-shirts..." are more adjacent than A admits; both are store-opening strategy angles with the same protagonist.
"Liquid Death certifies as a B Corp..." is clean but under-angled. It misses the tougher question of why a canned-water brand clearing B Corp standards is worth scrutiny.
gaps_in_B: "sells almost no water" is unsupported. The facts say merch, limited-edition canned water, and events; they do not give product mix or floor-share.
"stores they can't justify on unit economics" smuggles in an assumption. It may be a valid question, but the update gives no economics for the store.

"The standard just got a stress test" is a strong line, but it overstates what the supplied facts prove. It needs outside evidence that B Corp standards for packaged-water brands are actually contested.
"DTC/consumer-brands trade outlet" is slightly muddy for a brand already in ~120,000 retail doors. The retail-owned-store angle works; the DTC label is doing more costume than work.
